title: Serviceable archival for every configured development area
description:
Archival classifies each development area explicitly and stops refusing artifacts it was never meant to block, so a repository can archive a presentation deck through the supported workflow.

## Background

The archival planner refuses any selected root that is neither managed, permanent, nor already archived. The `[documentation]` block that repository initialization scaffolds is emitted commented out, names a subset of the areas under a development root, and advertises two keys the configuration type no longer carries. Policy completeness is computed from authored fields alone and ignores the runtime accessor fallbacks, so an adopter who never edits the scaffolded block gets an unconfigured policy and archival is refused whatever the fallbacks say.

Two further gaps compound it. A linked artifact outside the development root — source code, a script, an agent asset, a repository-root file — is blocked rather than archived by copy. A markdown link whose target resolves to a directory is treated as an unsupported artifact and blocks the plan that reaches it. Plan eligibility is all-or-nothing, so one blocker anywhere in a container subtree makes the whole plan ineligible.

Classification is explicit per area rather than a blanket rule over the development root, so an area holding living documentation archives by copy and retains its source while an area holding revision-specific work products moves.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A freshly initialized repository classifies every area under its development root as managed or permanent and reports a configured documentation policy without hand-editing.
- [hard] REQ-02: A presentation deck owned by a terminal issue previews as an eligible plan through both archive target forms, and no configured development area produces an unmanaged-selected-root blocker.
- [hard] REQ-03: A linked artifact outside the development root is classified permanent rather than blocked, and executing a plan that contains one relocates no file outside the development root.
- [hard] REQ-04: A link target that resolves to a directory produces no unsupported-artifact-type blocker, and a container whose remaining blockers were all directory targets yields an eligible plan.

planning.outcome: Development areas are explicitly classified and the planner stops blocking artifacts it should copy or skip.

title: Ship the development-area classification in the initialization scaffold
description:
The repository-initialization scaffold declares each development area as managed or permanent from one authoritative declaration, so a freshly initialized repository reports a configured documentation policy.

## Background

The documentation block the scaffold writes is commented out, covers a subset of the areas under a development root, and advertises two keys the configuration type no longer carries. Policy completeness is computed from authored fields alone, so an adopter who leaves the scaffolded block untouched gets an unconfigured policy and archival refuses to run. Making policy completeness honour the runtime fallbacks instead was rejected: it would change archive eligibility for every existing repository that has no authored table.

Classification is explicit per area. Areas holding revision-specific work products of terminal issues are managed and move on archive. Areas holding living documentation, a configured item-kind source, or documented invocation paths are permanent, archive by copy, and retain their source. Files that sit at the development root and belong to no area are classified individually as exact path entries, which the path matcher supports. A single entry for the development root itself is wrong, because matching is by path prefix and it would silently make every managed area permanent.

The declaration is configuration the tool writes for an adopter rather than engine policy, so it belongs in the scaffold instead of in classifier logic.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A repository created by initialization carries an authored documentation policy that names each development area as managed or permanent, with the presentation area managed and the architecture area permanent.
- [hard] REQ-02: The scaffolded documentation block is active configuration rather than commented-out guidance, and names only keys the configuration type carries.
- [hard] REQ-03: Development-root files that belong to no area are classified as exact path entries rather than swept in by a prefix.
- [hard] REQ-04: The managed and permanent area sets exist as one declaration that the scaffold emitter consumes, not as a restated literal list.
- [hard] REQ-05: Archive planning in a freshly initialized repository reports a configured policy status.

## Notes

The shipped classification is derived from initialization code and templates. This repository's live configuration is repository-local policy and is not the source of the shipped default.

title: Derive the runtime documentation defaults from the shipped declaration
description:
The runtime configuration accessors fall back to the same shipped area declaration the initialization scaffold writes, so the two can no longer disagree.

## Background

The documentation accessors return hard-coded fallback lists when no table is authored, and doc comments beside them restate those lists a second time. The scaffolded block, the accessor fallbacks, the adopter example configuration, and the adopter reference are four copies of one fact, and they already disagree with each other. Reducing them to one declaration removes the staleness defect rather than adding a fifth copy.

The fallbacks stay non-authorizing. Policy completeness is judged from authored fields alone, so a repository with no documentation table still reports an incomplete or unconfigured policy and archival still refuses to mutate. Changing that judgement is out of scope, because it would alter archive eligibility for existing repositories.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The managed-path, permanent-path, archive-root, and development-root fallbacks return values read from the shipped area declaration rather than from literals of their own.
- [hard] REQ-02: Doc comments describing the fallbacks carry no second copy of the path lists.
- [hard] REQ-03: A repository with no authored documentation table still reports an unconfigured or incomplete policy status, unchanged by the fallbacks.

title: Classify linked artifacts outside the development root as permanent
description:
A selected root that lies outside the configured development root is classified permanent instead of raising a blocker, so archival stops refusing plans over source files, scripts, agent assets, and repository-root documents.

## Background

The planner blocks a selected root that is neither managed, permanent, nor already archived, and returns no destination for it. Linked artifacts outside the development root fall into that gap: they are legitimately linked to terminal issues and archiving them by copy is the correct treatment, yet they defeat the whole plan because eligibility is all-or-nothing.

The relaxation is scoped to artifacts outside the configured development root, not to any artifact that matches no configured area. A blanket relaxation would turn a mistyped managed-path entry into silent copying with no diagnostic, discarding the signal the blocker exists to raise. Enumerating each outside root as permanent was rejected as a maintenance treadmill that re-blocks on the first unlisted root, and prefix matching would make an entry such as the crate source root permanent wholesale.

The classification policy value does not currently carry the development root, although the configuration accessor for it exists. Threading it in is the structural part of this work and stays inside the pure domain layer. The blocker code remains part of the stable wire vocabulary even though it fires less often; removing it would break the schema.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A selected root outside the configured development root is classified permanent and receives a destination instead of an unmanaged-selected-root blocker.
- [hard] REQ-02: A selected root inside the development root that matches no configured area still raises the blocker, so a mistyped area entry stays diagnosable.
- [hard] REQ-03: The classification policy value carries the configured development root, and the comparison uses that configured value rather than a built-in path literal.
- [hard] REQ-04: The unmanaged-selected-root code remains in the published blocker vocabulary.
- [hard] REQ-05: Adopter-facing command reference text describes the scoped behaviour.

planning.outcome: A selected root outside the configured development root classifies permanent instead of raising a blocker.

title: Guarantee archive execution retains sources outside the development root
description:
Executing a plan that contains an out-of-root linked artifact copies it into the mirror and leaves the original where it is, proven by regression coverage rather than by narration.

## Background

Permanent classification already implies a copy action, and a copy schedules no pending deletion, so source retention follows from the existing action model. That guarantee is currently unasserted: nothing fails if a future change turns one of those copies into a move and starts relocating source files, scripts, or agent assets out of the tree.

Because plan eligibility is all-or-nothing, the assertion is written against the retention property directly rather than against whole-plan eligibility, which can be false for unrelated reasons.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Executing a plan whose artifact set includes a linked file outside the development root leaves that file at its original path.
- [hard] REQ-02: The same execution publishes the mirrored copy under the archive root, so retention is not achieved by skipping the artifact.
- [hard] REQ-03: No pending deletion is scheduled for an artifact outside the development root.

title: Skip directory link targets during artifact discovery
description:
A markdown link whose target resolves to a directory is treated as navigation and skipped by artifact discovery, so it stops blocking the plans that reach it.

## Background

Artifact discovery follows document link edges and resolves each target. A trailing-slash link to a sibling directory resolves to something that is not a regular file, and the planner records it as an unsupported artifact with a blocking action. Index documents that link their sibling directories are legitimate markdown, and they are reached transitively as embedded artifacts from documents that are themselves linked, so the blockers land in container plans that have nothing to do with those index files. This is the largest blocker population in the repository and it is independent of any path classification.

Rewriting the offending links was rejected: they are valid markdown, one of the index documents is adopter-facing, and the defect would stay shipped for every adopter. Narrowing the cleanup criterion was rejected because it would leave the epic's acceptance evidence partial and the defect unrecorded.

A directory is navigation rather than a document, so skipping it is the correct semantics and not a suppression.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A link target that resolves to a directory produces no unsupported-artifact-type blocker and contributes no artifact entry.
- [hard] REQ-02: A link target that resolves to a regular file or symbolic link is unaffected.
- [hard] REQ-03: A container whose remaining blockers were all directory targets yields an eligible plan.
- [hard] REQ-04: Adopter-facing command reference text describes directory targets as navigation rather than as blocked artifacts.

planning.outcome: A link target that resolves to a directory is navigation and raises no unsupported-artifact-type blocker.

title: Adopt the shipped area classification in this repository's configuration
description:
This repository's documentation policy names the same managed and permanent areas as the shipped scaffold and declares its issue-scoped areas, so the cleanup that follows runs against the product's own default rather than a bespoke local table.

## Background

The change ships as a product default and this repository then adopts it. The live policy today names three managed areas and one permanent prefix, leaving eight areas under the development root unclassified. Adoption reclassifies them: work-product areas become managed and move on archive, while an area holding living contributor documentation, a configured item-kind source, or a documented invocation path becomes permanent and archives by copy. Development-root files that belong to no area are listed individually.

Adoption also declares which of the areas organize their artifacts by issue. That declaration is independent of the archival classification: a managed area that stays flat still archives its linked artifacts, and only the naming differs.

Adoption is what makes the repository-level acceptance evidence real, and it must land before any archival execution so that the executions run under the intended classification.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The repository documentation policy classifies each area under the development root as managed or permanent, matching the shipped declaration.
- [hard] REQ-02: Development-root files that belong to no area are listed as exact path entries.
- [hard] REQ-03: No entry covers the development root as a whole.
- [hard] REQ-04: The repository declares its issue-scoped areas as the active, study, plan, and presentation areas.
- [hard] REQ-05: The container candidate report shows no unmanaged-selected-root blocker for any area under the development root.

title: Canonical issue artifact directory convention
description:
An issue's artifacts live in one canonical directory derived from its identity inside an area configuration declares, resolved by a command that tooling and documentation call instead of spelling the pattern out.

## Background

Development artifacts are named as flat files at area root with the owning issue's short id as a filename prefix. The layout does not scale, and the one place that derives a directory name from an issue falls back to the issue title, which yields long names truncated mid-word.

The convention is a directory per issue named from the issue's membership label, falling back to a bare short id, with filenames inside the directory carrying no redundant short-id prefix. Only some areas under a development root organize their artifacts by issue, so configuration declares which ones do and every resolution names one of them. Directory-per-issue precedents already exist in the repository. The convention governs newly created artifacts; pre-existing flat files are tolerated rather than restructured in place.

Enforcement is a resolver plus an advisory report. A blocking validation rule was rejected because legacy flat artifacts are deliberately tolerated and a cutover predicate would be a false-positive source.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The development areas that adopt the convention are declared in configuration, and every canonical-directory resolution names one of them.
- [hard] REQ-02: An issue's canonical artifact directory is the named area joined with its short id and membership slug when the issue carries a membership label, and with the bare short id otherwise, with no name derived from an issue title.
- [hard] REQ-03: A command resolves the canonical directory, and tooling and documentation obtain the path from it rather than composing it from a spelled-out pattern.
- [hard] REQ-04: Artifact filenames inside an issue directory carry no short-id prefix.
- [hard] REQ-05: An advisory report lists artifacts under the declared issue-scoped areas that sit outside their owning issue's canonical directory, and the report blocks no state transition.

planning.outcome: One resolver, one command, and one advisory report establish the issue artifact directory convention.

title: Declare the development areas that adopt the issue directory convention
description:
Configuration declares which areas under the development root organize their artifacts by issue, so every path resolution names the area it wants instead of inferring one.

## Background

A development root holds many areas and only some of them are organized by issue. The rest hold living documentation, dated records, or generated output that no single issue owns. Configuration today declares one development root plus the managed and permanent path lists, and none of those answers which areas are issue-scoped. A resolver handed only an issue therefore cannot decide which area a new artifact belongs to, and any answer it invented would be a guess.

The registry is an explicit list of area paths. A resolver, a command, a template declaration, and a conformance report each name one of the registered areas and receive the issue-scoped directory inside it. Naming an area the registry does not declare is an error rather than a silently accepted path. The registry is also what the conformance report walks, so the scanned area set comes from configuration rather than from a built-in list.

Areas outside the registry keep their flat shape and are unaffected by the convention.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Configuration carries a declared list of the development areas that adopt the issue directory convention.
- [hard] REQ-02: An accessor returns the declared areas and falls back to a shipped default when no list is authored.
- [hard] REQ-03: Membership is queryable, so a caller can reject an area the registry does not declare.
- [hard] REQ-04: The repository-initialization scaffold emits the registry as active configuration rather than as commented-out guidance.
- [hard] REQ-05: The area paths appear once in the shipped default and nowhere else in engine logic.

## Notes

The shipped default is derived from initialization code and templates. This repository's live configuration is repository-local policy and is not the source of the shipped default.

title: Resolve an issue's canonical artifact directory inside a named area
description:
A pure domain function maps an issue and a registered issue-scoped area to the issue's canonical artifact directory in that area, so every consumer derives the path from one rule instead of restating it.

## Background

Two independent naming rules exist today and neither answers the question for a source-side artifact. The archival planner derives a destination directory from a membership label and falls back to the issue title; template interpolation composes a flat filename from a short id. The convention needs one derivation: the named area joined with the short id and the membership slug, or with the bare short id when no single membership value is available.

The area is an input rather than an inference. A development root holds several issue-scoped areas, so the caller states which one it wants and the function rejects an area the configured registry does not declare. What a caller never composes is the directory name itself.

Name precedence has three steps. Collect the issue's type labels; only when exactly one type label exists, look up that type's configured membership namespace; collect that namespace's values on the issue and only when exactly one exists, use it as the slug. Both ambiguous cases collapse to the bare short-id directory, which needs no new tie-breaking policy and matches the legacy directory shape the archival resolver already adopts.

The area set comes from the configured registry and the namespace from the configured type mapping, so the function carries no path literal. Slug normalization reuses the existing bounded, Unicode-safe slug helper rather than adding a second one. Legacy flat and suffix-form filenames stay resolvable; the function names where a new artifact belongs and never restructures an existing one.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: An issue with exactly one type label and exactly one value in that type's membership namespace resolves to the named area joined with its short id and that value's slug.
- [hard] REQ-02: An issue with no membership label, several type labels, or several membership values resolves to the named area joined with its bare short id.
- [hard] REQ-03: An area the configured registry does not declare produces a descriptive error rather than a resolved path.
- [hard] REQ-04: No resolved directory name is derived from an issue title.
- [hard] REQ-05: The area set is read from the configured registry and the membership namespace from the configured type mapping, with no path literal in the function.
- [hard] REQ-06: The function performs no input or output and reuses the existing slug normalizer.
- [hard] REQ-07: Resolving a directory for an issue whose artifacts are stored flat reports the canonical location and moves nothing.

planning.outcome: A pure function maps an issue and a named area to the issue's canonical artifact directory.

title: Expose the canonical artifact directory as a command
description:
A document subcommand prints an issue's canonical artifact directory in a named issue-scoped area, giving agents, scripts, and prose one place to obtain the path instead of composing it from a spelled-out pattern.

## Background

Nothing in the command surface derives a document path today; every document subcommand operates on a path the caller already knows. The archival group is defined as producing archival plans, so a pure path resolver does not belong there, while the document group already owns the document-path vocabulary.

The command takes the issue and the area it wants. Supplying the area is the caller's only contribution to the path; the directory name inside that area comes from the domain resolver. An area the configured registry does not declare is rejected with a descriptive error instead of producing a path.

The output is a single value, so it uses the established flat named-object shape for machine-readable output rather than the list envelope. Argument parsing and rendering stay in the command-line and output layers, orchestration in the command layer, and the derivation itself in the domain resolver.

Adding a command changes the generated bridge surface, which requires an explicit curation entry with a one-line rationale before its coverage check passes.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A subcommand accepts an issue identifier and an issue-scoped area, and prints the issue's canonical artifact directory in that area.
- [hard] REQ-02: An area the configured registry does not declare produces a descriptive error and a non-zero exit status.
- [hard] REQ-03: Machine-readable output is a flat named object carrying the issue identity, the named area, and the resolved path.
- [hard] REQ-04: An unknown issue identifier produces a descriptive error and a non-zero exit status rather than a fabricated path.
- [hard] REQ-05: The command is curated in the generated bridge manifest with a rationale.
- [hard] REQ-06: The adopter-facing command reference documents the subcommand and its area argument.

planning.outcome: A subcommand prints an issue's canonical artifact directory in human and machine-readable form.

title: Interpolate the canonical artifact directory into template document paths
description:
A graph template's document path can name the owning container's canonical artifact directory in an area the declaration states, so an instantiated template writes into the convention instead of a flat pattern.

## Background

Template document paths are interpolated from container fields, and the only field available for a path today is the short id, which forces every declaration to spell out a flat area-plus-prefix pattern. Two independent interpolation engines and one plan-document resolver consume the same field set, so exposing the directory once serves all of them.

Because a development root holds several issue-scoped areas, a declaration states which area its document belongs in and the interpolated field resolves the canonical directory inside that area. A declaration naming an area the configured registry does not declare fails at application time with a descriptive error rather than producing a path outside the convention.

The interpolated value is the resolved directory, so a declaration names a filename relative to it and that filename carries no short-id prefix.

title: Report artifacts sitting outside their owning issue's canonical directory
description:
A read-only report lists artifacts under the declared issue-scoped areas whose location disagrees with their owning issue's canonical directory, as advice rather than as enforcement.

## Background

Legacy flat artifacts are deliberately tolerated, so a blocking rule would be a false-positive source. A non-enforced validation rule would technically not block, but it rides inside the validation exit code that a repository gate consumes. A dedicated read-only report satisfies the non-blocking requirement by construction: a command that only prints cannot gate anything.

The report walks the issue-scoped areas the configuration registry declares, resolves each prefixed artifact's owning issue, compares its location with the canonical directory for the area it sits in, and lists the differences. An artifact whose owner cannot be resolved is reported as unattributed rather than as nonconforming. A shell-level area scan already exists in the repository as a precedent for this kind of advisory sweep, and it reads its root from configuration rather than hard-coding one.

title: Archive directory naming and citation breakage warnings
description:
The archival planner names its destination directory without falling back to an issue title and warns about in-content path citations that a move would break, without ever rewriting document content.

## Background

The planner derives a destination directory name from a membership label and falls back to the issue title when no single membership value exists. The fallback produces long names truncated mid-word, and one such directory exists in the archive as its own counter-example. Removing the fallback reverses a shipped, reviewed decision rather than fixing a bug; the reversal is deliberate.

Separately, the planner relinks issue document records when artifacts move, but it does not see path mentions in the text of ordinary files. Shell scripts, operator-facing error strings, a production module doc comment, adopter tutorials, and changelog entries all cite artifact paths inline, and none of them is a document link record, so validation stays silent when a move breaks them. Those citations must be reported as plan warnings.

Content is never rewritten. A citation inside a dated historical document must survive verbatim, so the planner warns and a human decides.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The archive directory name is derived from a membership label or a bare short id with no title fallback, and the one pre-existing title-slugged directory is renamed with its container marker still resolving it.
- [hard] REQ-02: An archival plan reports, as plan warnings, occurrences of a moving artifact's path in the text of tracked files anywhere in the repository, including code comments and shell scripts.
- [hard] REQ-03: Execution rewrites no document content.

planning.outcome: Archive directory names drop the title fallback and plans warn about in-content citations a move would break.

title: Derive the archive directory name without a title fallback

Destination naming has three steps: collect the issue's type labels, and only when exactly one exists look up its configured membership namespace; collect that namespace's values on the issue, and only when exactly one exists use it as the slug. Both ambiguous cases currently fall through to the issue title, which is normalized and cut at a fixed character bound with no word boundary, producing names truncated mid-word.

The replacement for the fallback is the bare short-id directory. It needs no new tie-breaking policy, it is the shape the resolver already adopts for legacy directories, and it converges on an existing supported form rather than inventing one.

This reverses a shipped, reviewed naming decision. The properties that make the reversal safe are also already shipped: a destination name is frozen at first archive and re-adopted by marker, and legacy identifier-only directories are adopted without data movement.

- [hard] REQ-02: An issue with several type labels, several membership values, or no membership label yields a destination directory named from the bare short id.
- [hard] REQ-03: No destination directory name is derived from an issue title.

title: Add a plan-warning code for in-content path citations

title: Warn on tracked-file occurrences of a moving artifact's path
description:
An archival plan reports a warning for each occurrence of a moving artifact's path in the text of a tracked file, anywhere in the repository, so a move that would break an inline citation is visible before it happens.

## Background

The planner reads structured document edges, which are link records and asset relationships, not mentions of a path in arbitrary prose or code. Matching only markdown link targets would reach a small minority of the citations that actually exist: it misses every shell-script line, an operator-facing error string, a production module doc comment, and both adopter-facing citations, all of which are inline code spans. Restricting the scan to the development root would miss the script and changelog citations entirely.

Evidence acquisition needs file bytes, so it belongs at the storage and planning boundary where other plan evidence is gathered, while constructing the warning stays pure. Untracked and ignored files are outside the scan.

title: Lock in that archive execution rewrites no document content
description:
Regression coverage proves that archival execution relocates and relinks artifacts without altering the bytes of any document, so the warning channel stays the only response to an inline citation.

## Background

Execution emits file writes, file deletions, and directory creations, and the only synthesized bytes it produces are the container marker. No content rewriting exists anywhere in the archival path, so the guarantee holds today but is unasserted. A citation inside a dated historical document must survive verbatim, which is why the planner warns instead of rewriting; without a regression test that boundary can erode silently.

The assertion distinguishes the two things execution legitimately changes — file location and the issue's document link records — from the one it must not change, which is file content.

- [hard] REQ-03: The issue document link records are still relinked to the new locations, so immutability is not achieved by skipping work.
- [hard] REQ-04: The container marker remains the only file whose bytes execution synthesizes.

title: Record a disposition for the unprefixed active-area design documents
description:

## Background

The active area holds design documents that predate the issue-prefix convention. Most already carry a document link to an owning issue, so their disposition is recorded rather than invented; a few carry none and need an individual call. Several are marked superseded by a banner in their own text and at least one is only partly superseded, which is why this area gets a per-file treatment instead of the blanket call the uniformly dated record areas take.

Three outcomes are available. An assigned owning issue makes an artifact archivable by the ordinary mechanism. A project-scoped reclassification keeps a document that describes standing project knowledge rather than one issue's work. An archived location retires a superseded document.

The files in this assignment are named individually so that each one's outcome is recorded and none is decided by inference from the group.
